title: UnityBC_understanding inequities in breast cancer
official: The UnityBC Study_understanding inequities in breast cancer
summary:
Background and study aims 
UnityBC (Understanding Inequities in Breast Cancer) is a new national research study funded by Cancer Research UK.

Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women, yet outcomes are not the same for everyone. Women from minority ethnic backgrounds are diagnosed with breast cancer less often than white women, but they generally have poorer outcomes. The reasons for this are not well understood, but could be related to differences in how women access healthcare or differences within the cancer itself.

Existing studies do not have enough women from key ethnic groups and information about the types of factors that affect the chances of developing breast cancer to answer these questions properly. In 2021, the largest ethnic groups among women included White British, Black African, Black Caribbean, Indian and Pakistani communities.

UnityBC is an observational study aiming to recruit a large, diverse, contemporary cohort of women with breast cancer from across the UK. By bringing together information on participants' health, lifestyle and experiences, diagnosis and treatment, the study aims to better understand why breast cancer outcomes differ between women from different ethnic backgrounds and generate evidence to help address observed differences.

The design and delivery of UnityBC is guided by a diverse group of patients and public volunteers, ensuring the study is relevant to women from all backgrounds.

Taking part in UnityBC means completing an online questionnaire. You can take part if you meet the inclusion criteria.
To join the study, please visit: https://www.ceu.ox.ac.uk/research/unitybc

Who can participate? 
All women aged 18 years and over who have been diagnosed with breast cancer within the previous 13 months. You can take part if you meet the inclusion criteria. To join the study, please visit: https://www.ceu.ox.ac.uk/research/unitybc

What does the study involve? 
Participation in UnityBC is online, and women will be able to self-refer to join through the UnityBC website (https://www.ceu.ox.ac.uk/research/unitybc). Participants will receive regular updates and become part of an active research community.

UnityBC will initially run for 12 months to test if it is working well and easy for women from diverse backgrounds to take part. Recruitment will focus on areas of the UK with more diverse populations, and results from the first 12 months will show us how best to reach and involve women from all backgrounds.

Eligible participants will complete online screening and provide informed consent via REDCap before completing a single online questionnaire about their background, breast cancer diagnosis, treatment, and experience of care. Data will be pseudonymised and stored securely. Descriptive statistics will be used to assess recruitment, questionnaire completion, and acceptability of future research participation and data sharing.

The study is coordinated by the Cancer Epidemiology Unit, Nuffield Department of Population Health, University of Oxford, UK.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating? 
Participants are not expected to receive any direct clinical benefit from taking part in UnityBC. However, some participants may find value in contributing their experiences and perspectives to research aimed at improving understanding of breast cancer among women from diverse backgrounds. Indirect benefits include the opportunity to contribute to the development of more inclusive and representative breast cancer research and to inform the design of future studies, services, and interventions that may better address inequalities in diagnosis, care, and outcomes.
The primary potential burdens relate to the time required to participate and the possibility of mild emotional discomfort when answering questions about a recent breast cancer diagnosis.
The time burden is minimal, as participation involves a single online consent process and completion of one questionnaire, expected to take approximately 30-40 minutes. Participants may complete the questionnaire at a time and place of their choosing and may pause or stop at any point.

Some questions may prompt reflection on personal experiences of breast cancer, which could cause transient distress. To minimise this risk, participants are clearly informed in advance about the nature of the questions and reminded that they may skip any questions they do not wish to answer or withdraw from the study at any time without providing a reason. Contact details for the study team are provided, and participants are encouraged to seek support from their usual care teams or support organisations if needed (details provided on the UnityBC website). No payments are offered, and participation will not affect current or future clinical care. Overall, the anticipated risks and burdens are minimal and proportionate to the aims of the study.

Where is the study run from?  
University of Oxford, UK.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for? 
August 2026 to July 2032.

Who is funding the study? 
Cancer Research UK.

Who is the main contact?
UnityBC Study Team, unitybc@ndph.ox.ac.uk

conditions: UnityBC will investigate why experiences and outcomes from breast cancer differ between women from various ethnic backgrounds in the UK.

interventions.name: UnityBC is a non-interventional observational study designed to collect information from women with breast cancer and aged over 18 years of age, from the five largest ethnic groups for women in the UK (White British, Indian, Pakistani, Black African, Black Caribbean) and other diverse backgrounds.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Women aged 18 years or over 
2. Diagnosed with breast cancer within the previous 13 months
3. Resident in the UK
Exclusion criteria:
1.	Male patients with breast cancer. We are excluding men from this study as the potentially small numbers will limit the ability to conduct any meaningful analyses.
2.	No access to an active email account
3.      No access to a computer, smartphone, or tablet with internet access (either directly or via a family member or friend)
